claim: C. chilonis has a close relationship with another braconid wasp, M. demolitor, with 75% amino acid identity in orthologous proteins
source: C. chilonis has a close relationship with another braconid wasp, M. demolitor, with 75% amino acid identity in orthologous proteins (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and stated in the text.

claim: C. chilonis was estimated to have diverged from M. demolitor approximately 61.05 (31.74–108.70) million years ago
source: C. chilonis was estimated to have diverged from M. demolitor approximately 61.05 (31.74–108.70) million years ago.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic divergence time estimation using MCMCtree.

claim: Synthesis capability for tryptophan, phenylalanine, tyrosine, and histidine was lost in holometabolous insects prior to hymenopteran divergence
source: Using comparative genomics, we find that synthesis capability for tryptophan, phenylalanine, tyrosine, and histidine was lost in holometabolous insects prior to hymenopteran divergence
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomic analysis across multiple species.

claim: Valine, leucine, and isoleucine synthesis capability was lost in the common ancestor of Hymenoptera
source: while valine, leucine, and isoleucine were lost in the common ancestor of Hymenoptera.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomic pathway analysis.

claim: Multiple loss events of lysine synthesis occurred independently in the Parasitoida and Aculeata
source: Subsequently, multiple loss events of lysine synthesis occurred independently in the Parasitoida and Aculeata.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing independent gene losses.

claim: C. chilonis has lost the ability to synthesize eight amino acids
source: Experiments in the parasitoid Cotesia chilonis confirm that it has lost the ability to synthesize eight amino acids.
evidence: The claim is supported by both genomic analysis and experimental feeding assays.

claim: Parasitoids account for about 75% of Hymenoptera species
source: Among the Hymenoptera, parasitoids account for about 75% of species and 10 ~ 20% of all insect species (Pennacchio and Strand, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Parasitoids account for 10-20% of all insect species
source: Among the Hymenoptera, parasitoids account for about 75% of species and 10 ~ 20% of all insect species (Pennacchio and Strand, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Parasitoids are important biological control agents in integrated pest management
source: They are also important biological control agents in integrated pest management (IPM) (Bale et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Female parasitoid wasps attack arthropod hosts and lay their eggs upon or within them
source: Female parasitoid wasps attack arthropod hosts and lay their eggs upon (ectoparasitoid) or within (endoparasitoid) them, where the offspring feed and develop, eventually causing host death.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about parasitoid biology.

claim: Parasitoid offspring feeding and development eventually causes host death
source: Female parasitoid wasps attack arthropod hosts and lay their eggs upon (ectoparasitoid) or within (endoparasitoid) them, where the offspring feed and develop, eventually causing host death.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about parasitoid biology.

claim: Parasitoids can manipulate the nutritional value of hosts through effectors such as venom proteins, polydnaviruses, and teratocytes
source: In addition, parasitoids can manipulate the nutritional value of the hosts through effectors injected into the host, such as venom proteins, polydnaviruses, and molecular factors produced by parasitoid cells (teratocytes) that are either injected into the host or produced by feeding larvae (Pennacchio and Strand, 2006; Pennacchio et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Parasitoid effectors alter host metabolism to mobilize nutrients from host tissues to meet the demands of developing larvae
source: As well as inhibiting host immunity and alterning host development, these mechanisms alter host metabolism in ways that mobilize nutrients from host tissues to meet the demands of developing larvae (Mrinalini et al., 2015; Pennacchio et al., 1995; Rivers and Denlinger, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some hemipteran insects have lost genes in amino acid biosynthetic pathways because they can obtain nutrition from their endosymbionts
source: For instance, some hemipteran insects have lost genes in amino acid biosynthetic pathways, apparently because they can obtain the nutrition from their endosymbionts (Douglas, 2006; Feldhaar, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Complete pathways of endosymbionts and incomplete pathways of insects have been confirmed in aphids, planthoppers, leafhoppers, and mealybugs
source: In some cases, this has been confirmed by annotation of the complete pathway of the endosymbiont and incomplete pathway of the insect, for instance in aphids (Richards et al., 2010), planthoppers (Xue et al., 2014), leafhoppers (McCutcheon and Moran, 2007), and mealybugs (Husnik and McCutcheon, 2016; Gil et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Parasitoid venoms induce a higher concentration of lipids in hosts
source: For example, parasitoid venoms induce a higher concentration of lipids, which is confirmed by in vitro injection of venom into the host (Nakamatsu and Tanaka, 2003; Nakamatsu and Tanaka, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Venom injected hosts of Nasonia vitripennis show dramatic alterations in host gene expression, sugar, chitin, and lipid metabolism, as well as elevation of free amino acid levels
source: Detailed transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses of venom injected hosts of Nasonia vitripennis reveal dramatic alterations in host gene expression (Martinson et al., 2014), sugar, chitin, and lipid metabolism, as well as elevation of free amino acid levels (Mrinalini et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nutritional components such as proteins, acylglycerols and free amino acids change in the hemolymph of parasitized pea aphid during development of Aphidius ervi larvae
source: To meet the demands of the developing wasp larvae, nutritional components such as proteins, acylglycerols and free amino acids change in the hemolymph of the parasitized pea aphid Acyrthosiphon pisum during development of parasitoid wasp Aphidius ervi larvae (Pennacchio et al., 1995; Rahbé et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Endoparasitoid wasp larvae absorb nutrients from host hemolymph through thin exoskeletons and epidermis at early stages
source: Previous studies showed that at early stages, endoparasitoid wasp larvae absorb nutrients from host hemolymph through thin exoskeletons and epidermis, whereas they absorb nutrients mainly through gut epithelium at later stages (Giordana et al., 2003; Caccia et al., 2005; Grimaldi et al., 2006; Pennacchio et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Endoparasitoid wasp larvae absorb nutrients mainly through gut epithelium at later stages
source: Previous studies showed that at early stages, endoparasitoid wasp larvae absorb nutrients from host hemolymph through thin exoskeletons and epidermis, whereas they absorb nutrients mainly through gut epithelium at later stages (Giordana et al., 2003; Caccia et al., 2005; Grimaldi et al., 2006; Pennacchio et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The C. chilonis genome was sequenced using Illumina HiSeq 2000 and PacBio platforms
source: Adopting a whole-genome shotgun sequence strategy and next-generation sequencing technologies, we used Illumina HiSeq 2000 and Pacbio platforms to sequence the genome of C. chilonis, supported by Novogene Bioinformatics Institute (Beijing, China).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement about the methods used.

claim: About 64.44 Gb of Illumina reads and 7.63 Gb of PacBio reads (~380 X coverage) were generated for C. chilonis genome sequencing
source: Finally, we generated about 64.44 Gb of Illumina reads and 7.63 Gb of Pacbio reads (~380 X coverage, Supplementary file 2 – Table 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data reported in the manuscript.

claim: The final C. chilonis genome assembly yielded 189 Mb of reference genomic sequence with a scaffold N50 of 2.2 Mb
source: The final assembly yielded 189 Mb of the reference genomic sequence with a scaffold N50 of 2.2 Mb.
evidence: The claim is supported by genome assembly statistics.

claim: 237 (95.6%) out of 248 CEGMA genes were represented in the C. chilonis genome assembly
source: We ran the core eukaryotic genes mapping approach (CEGMA) (version 2.4) to estimate the gene space (Parra et al., 2007), showing that 237 (95.6%) out of 248 CEGMA genes were represented in the genome assembly.
evidence: The claim is supported by CEGMA analysis results.

claim: 96.6% of 1658 Single-Copy BUSCOs (insecta_odb9) were complete in length in the C. chilonis genome
source: Evaluation using Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs (BUSCO) (version 3)confirmed the high quality of genome assembly (Simão et al., 2015), showing that 96.6% of 1658 Single-Copy BUSCOs (insecta_odb9) were complete in length (Supplementary file 2 – Table 11).
evidence: The claim is supported by BUSCO analysis results.

claim: 353,649 repeat sequences in a total of 68 Mb were predicted in the C. chilonis genome, constituting 36.18% of the genome
source: In total, we predicted 353,649 repeat sequences in a total of 68 Mb, which constitutes 36.18% of the C. chilonis genome (Supplementary file 2 – Tables 11–12).
evidence: The claim is supported by repeat sequence analysis.

claim: 14,142 protein-coding genes were identified in the C. chilonis genome
source: In total, OMIGA identified 14,142 protein-coding genes in the C. chilonis genome (Supplementary file 2 – Table 11).
evidence: The claim is supported by genome annotation results.

claim: C. chilonis clusters with four braconid wasps to form a group in the family Braconidae
source: Phylogenetic analysis by the maximum likelihood phylogenetic method showed that C. chilonis clusters with four braconid wasps, as expected, to form a group in the family Braconidae, a member of the superfamily Ichneumonoidea (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The superfamily Ichneumonoidea is a sister group to the superfamily Chalcidoidea
source: As previously established (Heraty, 2009; Misof et al., 2014; Peters et al., 2017), the superfamily Ichneumonoidea is a sister group to the superfamily Chalcidoidea
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous phylogenetic studies.

claim: Parasitoid wasps in Braconidae and Chalcidoidea are members of the infraorder Parasitoida
source: and the parasitoid wasps in Braconidae and Chalcidoidea are clustered together, and are members of the infraorder Parasitoida (Peters et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous phylogenetic study.

claim: The infraorder Parasitoida is a sister group to the infraorder Aculeata
source: which is a sister group to the infraorder Aculeata (containing vespid wasps, ants, and bees).
evidence: The claim is based on established phylogenetic relationships.

claim: Chromosomal rearrangement frequently occurred in various wasp species, especially after the divergence of C. chilonis and M. cingulum
source: We chose scaffolds that contain more than five genes for synteny analysis among three braconid wasps, and found that chromosomal rearrangement frequently occurred in various wasp species, especially after the divergence of C. chilonis and M. cingulum (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by synteny analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Seven pathway disruptions and 16 gene losses occurred in the common ancestor of Hymenoptera after their divergence from other holometabolous insects
source: Seven pathway disruptions and 16 gene losses have occurred in the common ancestor of Hymenoptera (Figure 2B, Figure 3) after their divergence from other holometabolous insects.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomic analysis shown in Figures 2B and 3.

claim: The disrupted pathways in the common ancestor of Hymenoptera are related to synthesis of cysteine, valine/leucine/isoleucine and arginine
source: These disrupted pathways are related to synthesis of cysteine (M00021 and M00609), valine/leucine/isoleucine (M00019, M00432 and M00570) and arginine (M00844 and M00029).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway analysis.

claim: 14 independent disruptions of amino acid synthetic pathways were documented within Hymenoptera, 10 in the Ichneumonoid/Chalcidoid clade and 4 in the Aculeata clade
source: Within the Hymenoptera, we have documented 14 independent disruptions of the amino acid synthetic pathways, 10 in the Ichneumonoid/Chalcidoid clade and 4 in the Aculeata clade, based on the genes involved and phylogenetic position of the species (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is no significant difference between the observed proportion of pathway disruptions in the Ichneumonoid/Chalcidoid clade (71%) and the expected proportion (55%)
source: There is no significantly difference between the observed proportion of pathway disruptions in the Ichneumonoid/Chalcidoid clade (71%) and the expected proportion (55%) (p=0.695, Fisher's exact test, N = 14).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: 164 independent gene losses were identified in Hymenoptera, 63 in the Aculeate clade and 77 in the Chalcidoid/Ichneumonoid clade
source: We also compared the frequency of gene losses within pathways, and identified a total of 164 independent gene losses, 63 in the Aculeate clade and 77 in the Chalcidoid/Ichneumonoid clade (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1 – Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Total gene losses show a similar frequency between the Ichneumonoid/Chalcidoid and Aculeate clades based on branch lengths
source: Total gene losses show a similar frequency between the Ichnuemonoid/Chalcidoid and Aculeate clades based on branch lengths (55% observed vs 55% expected compared to 45% vs 45% expected (p=1, Chi-square test, Supplementary file 2 – Table 1))
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Loss of M00030 is the direct cause of loss of capability to synthesize lysine, which independently happened nine times in Hymenoptera
source: Loss of M00030 is the direct cause of loss of capability to synthesize lysine, which independently happened nine times in Hymenoptera, five in the Ichneumonoid/Chalcidoid clade and four in the Aculeata clade.
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway analysis and phylogenetic inference.

claim: All lysine synthesis capability losses are due to loss of the same gene, aromatic amino acid aminotransferase I (ARO8, K00838)
source: All these are due to loss of the same gene in the M00030 pathway, aromatic amino acid aminotransferase I [EC:2.6.1.57 2.6.1.39 2.6.1.27 2.6.1.5] (ARO8, K00838) (Figure 2B, Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene loss analysis shown in Figures 2B and 3.

claim: The ARO8 gene was lost in nine Ichneumonoid wasps but retained in the braconid wasp Fopius arisanus
source: In the Ichneumonoidea, the ARO8 gene was lost in nine wasps, but retained in the braconid wasp Fopius arisanus.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomic analysis.

claim: The ARO8 gene can be found in Trichogramma pretiosum but cannot be detected in any other chalcidoid wasps in this analysis
source: This gene can be found in the earlier branch of Chalcidoidea, Trichogramma pretiosum, but cannot be detected in any other chalcidoid wasps in this analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomic analysis.

claim: 16 pathways were disrupted in the common ancestor of Holometabola, causing loss of biosynthesis in four amino acids
source: Examination of pathway completeness for seven species from three different orders of Holometabola (Coleoptera, Lepidoptera, and Diptera) revealed that 16 pathways were disrupted in the common ancestor of Holometabola (causing loss of biosynthesis in four amino acids).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative pathway analysis.

claim: Seven pathways were newly disrupted in the Hymenoptera after their divergence from other holometabolous insects, leading to a synthesis loss for three amino acids
source: Seven pathways were newly disrupted in the Hymenoptera after their divergence from other holometabolous insects (Figure 3), leading to a synthesis loss for three amino acids.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative pathway analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: 125 (76%) independent gene losses in Hymenoptera occurred in pathways that had already been disrupted in the common ancestor of Holometabola
source: There is a total of 125 (76%) independent gene losses in Hymenoptera for pathways that had already been disrupted in the common ancestor of Holometabola.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene loss analysis.

claim: The proportion of gene losses in already-disrupted pathways (76%) is significantly higher than the random expected proportion (52%)
source: This is significantly higher than the random expected proportion of gene losses (52%) estimated based on the gene number of each pathway in the ancestral state of Hymenoptera (p<0.01, df = 2, Chi-square test, Supplementary file 2 – Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Gene losses are more likely to occur in pathways which have already been disrupted in the common ancestor of Holometabola
source: This result suggested that gene losses are more likely to occur in pathways which have already been disrupted in the common ancestor of Holometabola.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the statistical analysis of gene loss patterns.

claim: The capabilities to synthesize histidine, tryptophan, tyrosine, and phenylalanine appear to have been lost early in holometabolous insects, prior to divergence of the basal Hymenoptera
source: The capabilities to synthesize histidine, tryptophan, tyrosine, and phenylalanine appear to have been lost early in holometabolous insects, prior to divergence of the basal Hymenoptera (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative pathway analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The capabilities to synthesize valine, leucine, and isoleucine were lost in the common ancestor of Hymenoptera after their divergence from other holometabolous insects
source: The capabilities to synthesize valine, leucine, and isoleucine were subsequently lost in the common ancestor of Hymenoptera after their divergence from other holometabolous insects (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative pathway analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The loss of valine, leucine, and isoleucine synthesis capability was due to the losses of two key genes: ketol-acid reductoisomerase (ilvC, K00053) and acetolactate synthase I/III small subunit (ilvH, K01653)
source: This was due to the losses of two key genes in the valine/leucine/isoleucine pathway, ketol-acid reductoisomerase [EC:1.1.1.86] (ilvC, K00053) and acetolactate synthase I/III small subunit [EC:2.2.1.6] (ilvH, K01653) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene loss analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 25 hymenopteran species lost the capability to synthesize lysine, 15 in the Ichneumonoid/Chalcidoid clade and 10 in the Aculeata clade
source: In this analysis, 25 hymenopteran species lost the capability to synthesize lysine, 15 in the Ichneumonoid/Chalcidoid clade and 10 in the Aculeata clade (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lysine synthesis capability losses are due to nine independent loss events, five in the Ichneumonoid/Chalcidoid clade and four in the Aculeata clade
source: Their phylogeny positions suggest these are due to nine independent loss events, five in the Ichneumonoid/Chalcidoid clade and four in the Aculeata clade.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic inference from the data.

claim: Synthesis loss was not found in Orussus or the sawflies
source: We did not find synthesis loss in Orussus or the sawflies.
evidence: The claim is based on pathway analysis results.

claim: Disruptions of the pathway from 3-phosphoserine to cysteine in some parasitoid lineages does not disrupt cysteine biosynthesis because it can be converted from L-cystathionine by CTH (K01758) in M00338
source: Disruptions of the pathway from 3-phosphoserine to cysteine in some parasitoid lineages caused by single gene loss does not disrupt the cysteine biosynthesis because it can be converted from L-cystathionine by CTH (K01758) in M00338 (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Different hymenopteran species show a total of 23–26 pathway disruptions, depending on whether loss of the lysine or/and cysteine pathways occurred within its lineage
source: Therefore, different hymenopteran species in our data set show a total of 23–26 pathway disruptions, depending on whether loss of the lysine (M00030, M00433) or/and cysteine (from 3-phosphoserine to cysteine) pathways occurred within its lineage.
evidence: The claim is based on pathway analysis across species.

claim: The number of synthesis capability losses in hymenopterans ranged from seven to eight, depending on whether lysine synthesis capability was lost
source: The number of synthesis capability losses ranged from seven to eight, depending on whether lysine synthesis capability, due to disruption in the lysine pathway M00030, occurred in a particular lineage.
evidence: The claim is based on pathway analysis across species.

claim: C. chilonis showed 24 pathway disruptions, 23 of them occurred basally in Hymenoptera or earlier, and one (M00030) happened in the common ancestor of Cotesia, Microplitis and Macrocentrus
source: In C. chilonis, our analysis showed 24 pathway disruptions, 23 of them occurred basally in Hymenoptera or earlier, and the remaining one (M00030) happened in the common ancestor of Cotesia, Microplitis and Macrocentrus.
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway analysis for C. chilonis.

claim: Pathway losses in C. chilonis disrupted the biosynthesis of eight amino acids: lysine, tryptophan, phenylalanine, tyrosine, isoleucine, leucine, valine, and histidine
source: These pathway losses disrupted the biosynthesis of eight amino acids (lysine, tryptophan, phenylalanine, tyrosine, isoleucine, leucine, valine, and histidine) (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 2 – Table 4, Table 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 46 genes were found to be missing in the amino acid biosynthesis pathway for C. chilonis
source: In total, 46 genes were found to be missing in the amino acid biosynthesis pathway for C. chilonis, thus disrupting the biosynthesis of eight amino acids (Lys, Trp, Phe, Tyr, Ile, Leu, Val, His).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene loss analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The genes related to the biosynthesis of three essential amino acids (arginine, methionine and threonine) were not lost in C. chilonis
source: The genes related to the biosynthesis of three other essential amino acids (arginine, methionine and threonine) were not lost.
evidence: The claim is based on pathway analysis.

claim: For methionine and threonine, although the biosynthetic pathways from aspartate were broken by some gene loss, these amino acids can be synthesized from serine
source: For methionine and threonine, although the biosynthetic pathways from aspartate were broken by some gene loss, these amino acids can be synthesized from another non-essential amino acid, serine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: All genes in the pathway from serine to methionine and threonine could be expressed in at least one stage during C. chilonis development
source: The expression of genes in the pathway from serine to methionine and threonine also were examined using RNA-seq data, and it was found that all genes could be expressed in at least one stage during wasp development.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq expression data.

claim: The 5-methyltetrahydrofolate-homocysteine methyltransferase (metH) gene in C. chilonis was only expressed in later larvae and adults
source: Interestingly, the 5-methyltetrahydrofolate-homocysteine methyltransferase (metH; EC: 2.1.1.13) gene in the last step to synthesize methionine was only expressed in later larvae and adults, which means C. chilonis cannot synthesize methionine by itself in early larval and pupal stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: For arginine, the biosynthetic pathway from glutamate to arginine (M00845) was broken, but the pathway from ornithine to arginine (M00844) was complete with gene expression at different life stages
source: For arginine, the biosynthetic pathway from glutamate to arginine (KEGG module: M00845) was broken, but the pathway from ornithine to arginine (KEGG module: M00844) was complete with gene expression at different life stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway and expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: C. chilonis can synthesize arginine, threonine, and methionine from a genomic point of view (but for methionine, only at later larval and adult stages)
source: These results indicate that, from a genomic point of view, C. chilonis can synthesize arginine, threonine, and methionine (but for methionine, only at later larval and adult stages).
evidence: The claim is an inference from pathway and expression analysis.

claim: The absence of any of the eight amino acids (lysine, tryptophan, phenylalanine, tyrosine, leucine, isoleucine, valine, and histidine) led to developmental arrest of C. chilonis larvae
source: The results indicated that the absence of any of the eight amino acids mentioned above led to developmental arrest of parasitoid larvae, demonstrating that C. chilonis larvae cannot survive in the medium without each of these eight amino acids.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro feeding assay results.

claim: C. chilonis larvae could survive in the medium without glycine
source: However, they could survive in the medium without glycine, presumably because they can synthesize it (based on the pathway analysis, Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro feeding assay results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: All eight amino acids that C. chilonis cannot synthesize were represented in the hemolymph of non-parasitized C. suppressalis larvae
source: In the non-parasitized C. suppressalis larvae, all eight amino acids were represented in the hemolymph.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic analysis.

claim: Histidine was the most abundant amino acid in non-parasitized C. suppressalis hemolymph at a concentration of 4.455 mg/ml
source: Histidine was the most abundant at a concentration of 4.455 mg/ml, followed by glutamine at a concentration of 3.262 mg/ml (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In parasitized C. suppressalis larvae, the amounts of four amino acids (arginine, serine, tyrosine, and alanine) were significantly increased in the first 3 days after parasitism
source: In the parasitized larvae, the amounts of four amino acids (arginine, serine, tyrosine, and alanine) were significantly increased and four amino acids (5-hydroxylysine, glutamic acid, methionine, and lysine) were significantly decreased in the first 3 days after parasitism (p<0.05, Student's t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Four amino acids (5-hydroxylysine, glutamic acid, methionine, and lysine) were significantly decreased in parasitized C. suppressalis hemolymph in the first 3 days after parasitism
source: In the parasitized larvae, the amounts of four amino acids (arginine, serine, tyrosine, and alanine) were significantly increased and four amino acids (5-hydroxylysine, glutamic acid, methionine, and lysine) were significantly decreased in the first 3 days after parasitism (p<0.05, Student's t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Lysine was significantly decreased in the host hemolymph in the first 3 days after parasitism
source: Among the eight amino acids that C. chilonis cannot synthesize by itself, lysine was found to be significantly decreased in the host hemolymph in the first 3 days after parasitism, likely resulting from the absorption of lysine by the wasp larvae.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic analysis.

claim: Tyrosine was significantly increased in host hemolymph in the first 3 days after parasitism
source: However, tyrosine was significantly increased in the first 3 days after parasitism
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic analysis.

claim: Levels of six amino acids (valine, tryptophan, histidine, phenylalanine, isoleucine, and leucine) were not significantly changed in host hemolymph after parasitism
source: while levels of six other amino acids (valine, tryptophan, histidine, phenylalanine, isoleucine, and leucine) were not significantly changed in the hemolymph.
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic analysis.

claim: 16 protease genes were significantly upregulated (4–59-fold) in fat body and hemolymph of the host following parasitism
source: It was found that 16 protease genes were significantly upregulated (4–59-fold) in fat body and hemolymph of the host following parasitism (Supplementary file 2 – Table 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome analysis.

claim: Most upregulated proteases were genes encoding serine proteases, trypsins and carboxypeptidases
source: Most were the genes encoding serine proteases, trypsins and carboxypeptidases, which play important roles in proteolysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome analysis and known functions of these enzymes.

claim: Parasitism does not have significant influence on host's amino acid biosynthetic pathways, as the expression of most genes (82%) in the pathways were not changed significantly after parasitism
source: In addition, parasitism does not have significant influence on host's amino acid biosynthetic pathways, as the expression of most genes (82%) in the pathways were not changed significantly after parasitism (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only six genes in host amino acid biosynthetic pathways were found to be significantly downregulated in the fat body after parasitism
source: Only six genes were found to be significantly downregulated in the fat body.
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome analysis.

claim: Five genes in the amino acid biosynthetic pathway were significantly upregulated after parasitism, all of which also belong to glycolysis and citrate cycle
source: Interestingly, we found that five genes in the amino acid biosynthetic pathway were significantly upregulated after parasitism. All of them are also belong to glycolysis (M00002) and citrate cycle (M00010) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 103 ABC transporter genes were identified in the C. chilonis genome
source: In total, 103 ABC transporter genes were identified in the C. chilonis genome.
evidence: The claim is supported by genome annotation.

claim: The ABC transporters gene family showed expansion in C. chilonis compared with other hymenopteran insects
source: Compared with other hymenopteran insects, the ABC transporters gene family showed expansion in C. chilonis, as revealed by maximum likelihood phylogenetic analysis (Figure 6A, Supplementary file 2 – Table 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: M. demolitor, the closest relative of C. chilonis in the study, only has 51 ABC transporters in the genome
source: In contrast, M. demolitor, the closest relative of C. chilonis in our study, only has 51 ABC transporters in the genome.
evidence: The claim is supported by genome annotation.

claim: The expansion of ABC transporters occurred after divergence of C. chilonis and M. demolitor
source: This result indicates that the expansion of ABC transporters occurred after divergence of C. chilonis and M. demolitor (Supplementary file 2 – Table 7).
evidence: The claim is an inference from comparative genomic data.

claim: 36 ABC transporters were more highly expressed in the larval stage relative to the pupal stage in C. chilonis (FoldChange (FPKM) >2)
source: We found 36 ABC transporters were more highly expressed in the larval stage relative to the pupal stage (FoldChange (FPKM) >2).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome analysis.

claim: Ten putative APCs and eight putative AAAPs were identified in the C. chilonis genome
source: Ten putative APCs and eight putative AAAPs were identified in the C. chilonis genome (Supplementary file 2 – Table 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by genome annotation.

claim: Two APC genes were highly expressed in the larval stage relative to the pupal and adult stages in C. chilonis
source: Although phylogenetic analysis showed that the APC gene family was not significantly expanded, transcriptome analysis results indicate that two APC genes were highly expressed in the larval stage relative to the pupal and adult stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome analysis.

claim: Five APC genes were highly expressed in the larval and pupal stages relative to the adult stage in C. chilonis
source: Five APC genes were highly expressed in the larval and pupal stages relative to the adult stage (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Only one AAAP gene was highly expressed in larvae of C. chilonis
source: However, only one AAAP gene was highly expressed in larvae (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expansion of ABC transporters in C. chilonis is an independent event, as it was not found in close relatives
source: This finding suggests that the expansion of ABC transporters in C. chilonis is an independent event, as it was not found in close relatives.
evidence: The claim is an inference from comparative genomic analysis.

claim: ABC transporter expansion events also independently occurred in the sawfly Cephus cinctus, some ants, Megachile bees and Bombus bees
source: The expansion events also independently occurred in the sawfly Cephus cinctus, some ants, Megachile bees and Bombus bees.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Some host amino acid transporters, such as vacuolar amino acid transporters, vesicular glutamate transporters, and proton-coupled amino acid transporter-like proteins, were significantly upregulated after parasitism
source: Interestingly, some host amino acid transporters, such as vacuolar amino acid transporters, vesicular glutamate transporters, and proton-coupled amino acid transporter-like proteins, were significantly upregulated after parasitism (Supplementary file 2 – Table 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptome analysis.

claim: The majority of amino acid synthesis losses occurred basally in the holometabolous insects and early in hymenopteran evolution
source: However, the majority of amino acid synthesis losses occurred basally in the holometabolous insects and early in hymenopteran evolution.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the comparative genomic analysis results.

claim: All hymenopterans appear to lack the capability to synthesize seven amino acids (four were lost earlier in holometabolous insects and three were lost in the common ancestor of Hymenoptera)
source: In this study, we found that all hymenopterans appear to lack the capability to synthesize seven amino acids (four were lost earlier in holometabolous insects and three were lost in the common ancestor of Hymenoptera)
evidence: The claim is a summary of the comparative genomic analysis results.

claim: Some parasitoids and aculeates have additionally lost the capability to synthesize lysine
source: and some parasitoids and aculeates have additionally lost the capability to synthesize lysine.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the comparative genomic analysis results.

claim: The trait loss of lysine biosynthesis in parasitoid wasps may implicate their amino-acid-rich diet combined with the capability of parasitoids to manipulate the nutritional quality of hosts
source: The trait loss of lysine biosynthesis in parasitoid wasps may implicate their amino-acid-rich diet combined with the capability of parasitoids to manipulate the nutritional quality of hosts through venoms and other means.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: The trait loss in aculeates may reflect their specialized diets, such as bees feeding on amino acid rich pollen and ants having a wide range of food sources
source: The trait loss in aculeates also may reflect their specialized diets. For example, bees feed on amino acid rich pollen and ants have a wide range of food sources (Rabie et al., 1983; Nicolson and Human, 2013).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Symbiotic bacteria can provide essential nutrients to host insects, as reported in Cephalotes ants and aphids
source: Another possibility is that symbiotic bacteria can provide essential nutrients to host insects, as reported in Cephalotes ants by Hu et al., 2018 and as well known in other insects such as aphids (Wilson et al., 2010; Feng et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Intracellular bacteria Buchnera significantly contributes to parasitoid host nutritional suitability
source: Previous studies indicate that intracellular bacteria Buchnera (symbiotic bacteria of aphids) significantly contributes to parasitoid host nutritional suitability (Pennacchio et al., 1999; Rahbé et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The synthesis capability of lysine was lost in the common ancestor of two aphid parasitoids A. ervi and L. fabarum
source: In our study, the synthesis capability of lysine was found to be lost in the common ancestor of two aphid parasitoids A. ervi and L. fabarum.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative genomic analysis.

claim: The lysine synthesis loss in aphid parasitoids may be associated with their parasitoid relationship with aphids, which possess intracellular bacteria that provide amino acids to the host
source: This phenomenon may be associated with their parasitoid relationship with aphids, which possess intracellular bacteria that provide amino acids to the host (Wilson et al., 2010; Feng et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Parasitism can alter the host's metabolic system and release nutrients into hemolymph to increase nutritional suitability for parasitoid through venoms, teratocytes and parasitoid larval feeding
source: Previous studies have reported that parasitism can alter the host's metabolic system and release nutrients into hemolymph to increase nutritional suitability for parasitoid through venoms, teratocytes and parasitoid larval feeding (Digilio et al., 2000; Nakamatsu and Tanaka, 2003; Nakamatsu and Tanaka, 2004; Caccia et al., 2005; Falabella et al., 2005; Falabella et al., 2007; Falabella et al., 2009; Caccia et al., 2012; Mrinalini et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Many previous studies have demonstrated in vitro that some essential amino acids are supplied by the host to parasitoid wasps
source: Many previous studies have demonstrated in vitro that some essential amino acids, which are of considerable importance in the nutritional and metabolic adaptations of parasitoid wasps, are supplied by the host (Giordana et al., 2003; Caccia et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The capability to synthesize four amino acids (histidine, tryptophan, tyrosine, and phenylalanine) was lost early in holometabolous insects, prior to divergence of the basal Hymenoptera
source: Among these eight amino acids, the capability to synthesize four amino acids (histidine, tryptophan, tyrosine, and phenylalanine) was lost early in holometabolous insects, prior to divergence of the basal Hymenoptera.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the comparative genomic analysis results.

claim: The synthetic capability of three amino acids (valine, leucine and isoleucine) was subsequently lost in the common ancestor of Hymenoptera
source: The synthetic capability of additional three amino acids (valine, leucine and isoleucine) was subsequently lost in the common ancestor of Hymenoptera.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the comparative genomic analysis results.

claim: The capability to synthesize lysine was lost in the common ancestor of Cotesia, Microplitis and Macrocentrus
source: The capability to synthesize lysine was lost in the common ancestor of Cotesia, Microplitis and Macrocentrus (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Parasitism by C. chilonis significantly changed the levels of various amino acids in host hemolymph
source: The metabolomic analysis showed that parasitism by C. chilonis significantly changed the levels of various amino acids in host hemolymph (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Early larvae parasitoids may largely absorb lysine in host hemolymph, since lysine is essential for parasitoid development
source: This result suggests that early larvae parasitoids may largely absorb lysine in host hemolymph, since lysine is essential for parasitoid development.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the metabolomic data.

claim: Venom and/or other effectors produced by parasitoids significantly increase the concentration of tyrosine in host hemolymph
source: In addition, venom and/or other effectors produced by parasitoids (i.e. PDV, teratocytes), and/or by larvae feeding significantly increase the concentration of tyrosine in host hemolymph, but parasitoid larvae utilize only a small amount of tyrosine at early stages (3 days after parasitism).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the metabolomic data.

claim: Parasitoid larvae utilize only a small amount of tyrosine at early stages (3 days after parasitism)
source: In addition, venom and/or other effectors produced by parasitoids (i.e. PDV, teratocytes), and/or by larvae feeding significantly increase the concentration of tyrosine in host hemolymph, but parasitoid larvae utilize only a small amount of tyrosine at early stages (3 days after parasitism).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the metabolomic data.
